insider_note: Tightly bound against loosely bound is the difference between the first two types. Say 'tightly' and 'loosely' in those words — it is the fastest way to show you know the contrast.

steps.label: What a cofactor is
steps.margin_note: Three named parts and the three types. This mark is vocabulary.
lines: An enzyme with its non-protein part is called a
The protein part is the APOENZYME.
The NON-PROTEIN part is the CO-FACTOR.
steps.why: A cofactor is defined by what it is not — not protein — so the apoenzyme and holoenzyme have to be named first for the definition to mean anything.
common_mistakes: Calling the cofactor the protein part. It is the NON-protein part.
Mixing up apoenzyme and holoenzyme. Apo is the protein alone; holo is the whole working enzyme.
steps.memory_tip: Apo is the protein, holo is the whole, cofactor is the rest.

steps.label: Prosthetic groups
steps.margin_note: Tightly bound, one example, the equation. The word 'tightly' is the mark.
lines: Organic compounds TIGHTLY bound to the
Example: the haem part of peroxidase.
Peroxidase breaks hydrogen peroxide into water
steps.why: Being tightly bound means the group stays with the enzyme through the reaction, which is the one thing that separates it from a coenzyme.
common_mistakes: Saying prosthetic groups are loosely bound. They are TIGHTLY bound.
Naming no example. Haem in peroxidase is the standard one.
steps.memory_tip: Prosthetic is permanent: it does not leave the enzyme.

steps.label: Co-enzymes
steps.margin_note: Loosely attached, the vitamin origin, one example with the vitamin named.
lines: Organic compounds LOOSELY attached to the
They are derived from water soluble vitamins.
Example: NAD and NADP both contain the vitamin
steps.why: A loosely attached coenzyme can leave, carry something away and come back, which is exactly what NAD does when it carries hydrogen between reactions.
common_mistakes: Saying coenzymes are tightly bound. They are LOOSELY attached.
Leaving out the vitamin link. Coenzymes come from water soluble vitamins.
steps.memory_tip: Coenzymes come and go, and they come from vitamins.

steps.label: Metal ions
steps.margin_note: Say where the ion binds and give the named example.

lines.text: Tightly bound, loosely bound, or a metal ion

lines: Many enzymes need metal ions to work.
The ion forms coordination bonds with side
Example: zinc is the cofactor for the
steps.why: A metal ion is inorganic, so it is neither a prosthetic group nor a coenzyme and needs a third category of its own.
common_mistakes: Calling metal ions organic. They are INORGANIC, which is why they are a separate type.
Naming no example. Zinc with carboxypeptidase is the standard one.
steps.memory_tip: Two organic types and one metal: that is the whole list.
